en: When the king passed away,
Wandering to Bukhara,
My poor elder sister Kanykey
Had become destitute.
Weeping, speaking, taking the direct path,
Calling her own child ‘younger brother,’
Your impassioned mother Kanykey
Led Semetey along.
On the ridge of great Bukhara,
Your dear elder sister Kanykey,
Though she was a widow,
Did not abandon her rank as khan.
Seven hundred households were under her hand.
The reason they were under her hand—
Dividing her hair behind into ten,
Was she not your sister-in-law who braided it?
While her Magnanimous One lived,
Reaching out to all the world's people,
Was she not your sister-in-law accustomed to it?
Who had learned from Manas,
Was she not your skillful sister-in-law?
A tigress among the people,
Was she not your mighty sister-in-law?
Walking slowly, taking the direct path,
Her orphan clear as glass,
Without revealing she was his mother,
She led him, calling him ‘younger brother.’
When he stopped, in distress,
She pleaded, ‘Little brother.’
Kanykey's white palace,
Its doors iron, solid tin,
Though she was a widow,
Its splendor was far greater.
Fierce men bearing iron-headed maces,
There were four to guard the gate.
From the skillful spearmen,
From the unsparing mighty men,
Farther on there were six.
Marksmen who never missed,
Tall and broad-shouldered,
Wrestlers and lions alike,
There were seven guards.
A brass post with a golden band,
She had it driven in by the threshold.
Every part of them well formed,
Akborchuk and Taytoru
Stood tethered there.
The dear lion, proud as a rooster,
Firmly turning his thoughts,
Pleading hard, calling him ‘younger brother,’
She kept deceiving her son.
At the entrance to the white palace,
She quietly took his horse.
Kanykey walked over,
Long accustomed to seeing guests off,
Your dear, dauntless mother,
Among the swift steeds,
Tethered Aktulpar.
Into Kanykey's palace,
The carefree boy,
She led him along.
The gate had a cord.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Pulled it with a clang.
Making herself known as his elder sister,
Into the palace like paradise,
She brought Semetey.
After the boy entered the palace:
‘My orphan left by my khan,
Will not turn and come back out,’ she said.
‘He will not hear my wailing voice,’ she said.
When Semetey entered that house,
The steel door, the great gate,
Once fastened, could never open.
The valiant one's cord,
She fastened it with a clang,
And shut the boy inside.
The poor king's wife
Now raised a screaming cry.
From her dear quail-like eyes,
Tears fell drop after drop.
From her dear currant-like eyes,
Tears streamed a whip's length.
She wept and screamed.
To God whose decree is mighty,
Your dear mother Kanykey
Sobbed in prayer:
“The dear bird called a wild duck
Wheels in flight toward the steppe.
How much was I to endure, ah,
God, for the child born from my womb!
The dear bird called a little bustard
Flies swiftly for food.
I was to bear hardship, ah,
For you, left by the valiant one.
I let a bird devour the swan,
The orphan born from my womb,
The light left by my companion.
Oh God, what shall I do with this grief?
You had him called the son of Sarts.
What shall I do, God, a grievous ordeal,
You let a bird devour the goose.
The orphan born from my womb,
When I fled to Bukhara,
You had him called another man's son.
God, you have shattered my thoughts.
You had him called another man's son,
This child who came from my body.
The steed poised to spring,
You made me call him ‘little brother,’
The light bestowed by fortune.
You have divided my thoughts every way.
You had him called other men's son,
My dear one God,
My boy left by the Magnanimous One.
You closed the wide world and made it narrow.
My boy bestowed by fate,
My dear one God,
You made me yearn for a single sight of him.
Let me scream and weep,
My dear one God,
Sitting here weeping in earnest,
What desire shall I attain?
‘He may happen to hear my screaming voice,’ I think.
‘My orphan may be unable to bear it and come out,’ I think.
Digging my pit deep,
If he should happen to suspect,
Will he make my misery boil?
May he not bring upon my head
A calamity no person would inflict.”
Speaking thus, Kanykey,
The tears from her quail-like eyes,
Now wiped them separately.
Her tears a whip's length,
Your dear mother Kanykey,
Turned and wiped them away.
The white palace with iron doors,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Went back inside.
Then the boy Semetey,
The boy stood bewildered, not moving.
Your royal, impassioned mother's
Vast, well-ordered possessions,
The boy regarded with troubled wonder.
Beyond the edge of the threshold,
He had not yet passed.
The gold-patterned carpet,
The noble orphan boy
Had not yet stepped upon.
If you look on this side,
It was carved from ruby,
Satisfying the heart of anyone who saw it.
With no difference between day and night,
She had it made bright.
If you look on this side,
It was cut from pure gold.
If you look at the place of honor,
All gold, countless gold coins,
Each laid in its proper place.
If you look over on this side,
The kettle was gold, the grain cheap.
The tablecloth was spread,
Sugar heaped like snow,
With great chunks of butter,
To anyone entering with joy,
It revealed a vision of paradise.
My poor elder sister Kanykei
Had taken a weaned lamb, its sweet head,
And boiled it tender.
She sliced rump meat and set out neck fat;
Upon the tablecloth
She laid seventy kinds of food.
The very sight filled the heart;
All those foods
She set out for Semetey to eat.
Through her thoughtful arrangements,
Every one of her chests
She filled with treasures of yellow gold.
She has costly goods and resources;
She has red gold as well.
Even if she faced hardship for forty years,
This whole Bukhara,
My precious elder sister Kanykei
Has the means to buy.
When my brother-in-law Manas was alive,
Great heaps of wealth were gathered.
In Bukhara, Temir Khan and Shaatemir,
Koloykan and Ismail—
The wealth of these four,
If we gathered every bit of it,
Would not equal even one portion of my sister’s.
When my brother-in-law Manas was alive,
What a woman my elder sister must have been!
My brother-in-law who married this sister of mine—
What complaint could he have against God?
Of the ravine running down this hillside,
Would that I became the spring!
Of Manas, who has gone to the other world,
Would that I, poor soul, became
The only child won through such suffering!
This Kara-Kyr stretched out before us—
Ah, would that it became my line for tethering foals!
This precious elder sister Kanykei—
Would that, instead of my sister,
She became my mother!
If I were Manas’s son,
If I were my sister’s camel calf,
There would be heaps of gathered wealth;
Against Almighty God,
Ah, I would have no complaint at all.
From my generous brother-in-law Manas’s
White loins, would that I had sprung!
My precious elder sister Kanykei—
Would that I had kicked my way out of her womb!
For Manas to ride for six months,
Would that I became his swift steed!
Of this precious, unfortunate mother,
The only son won through such suffering—
Would that I became her lamp!
If I were Manas’s son,
If I were my sister’s only child,
My heart would be content at the thought;
Against Almighty God
I would have no complaint at all!
This unlucky elder sister of mine
Is not one who should be left childless;
How could she have been left childless?
My brother-in-law gone to the other world
Is not a khan who should be left without a calf;
How could he have been left without a calf?
What God decrees
Leaves one helpless.
This sister of mine who weeps—
By my stately brother-in-law Manas,
How was she left ‘childless’?”
His heart smoldered with grief;
Unable to bear looking on,
Semetey grieved.
Saying he would go hawking, Semetey
Rode out from Bukhara,
Semetey grieving still more,
His precious eyes, like a saker falcon’s,
Filled with tears without blinking.
Mournful, unable to take heart,
Semetey turned back
And burst into deep, resounding sobs.
Once, Kanykei had come in mourning,
Semetey had fled to Bukhara.
Kanykei had come a widow,
Semetey had come a wanderer.
Plundering riches, they prospered,
The fierce one had entered Bukhara and grown,
A lion champion upheld by his patron,
His twelve limbs all in proportion,
Manas, who had gone to the other world—
He had become a warrior to match him.
